outline.description: Sets out the factual narrative of the petitioners’ experiences in Colombia and traces the immigration proceedings from the IJ through the BIA to the Tenth Circuit.
subtopics: Parties: Colombian nationals Jimenez, Duarte, and two minor children
Key facts: Liberal Party activity; 2022 campaign work for Federico Gutiérrez
Events with Don Rafa: property dispute, discovery of criminal activity, threats, armed confrontation at factory, threat to child, temporary move to countryside
Limited interactions with police and alleged comment about futility
Procedural history: NTA and removability; asylum/withholding/CAT applications; IJ credibility finding but denial; BIA affirmance; issues preserved on appeal (asylum and withholding only)

outline.chapter_title: Standards of Review and Governing Legal Framework
outline.description: Explains the court’s jurisdiction, record-based review, and the legal standards for asylum and withholding, including the substantial evidence standard and the elements of past persecution.
subtopics: Jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252; review limited to administrative record
Review posture: single-member BIA decision with reference to IJ’s reasoning
Substantial evidence standard: findings conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to disagree
Asylum eligibility: refugee definition under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A)
Past persecution route to presumption of future persecution
Three asylum elements: persecution, nexus to protected ground, government unable or unwilling to control
Withholding of removal: higher burden; rises and falls with failure to establish well-founded fear in asylum
Mixed-motive principle: protected ground must be at least one central reason

outline.description: Analyzes whether the petitioners’ experiences amount to persecution under Tenth Circuit precedent when viewed cumulatively.
subtopics: Definition and contours: persecution requires more than restrictions or threats to life and liberty
Cumulative assessment of incidents: threatening calls and brochure; armed threat at factory; assault on employee; near-abduction scare involving child
Concession of no physical injury and lack of lasting physical harm
Emotional and psychological harm claims (insomnia, panic attacks) and the court’s treatment of such harms without accompanying severe physical harm
Comparative case law: threats alone insufficient (Karki); more extreme fact patterns found insufficient in unpublished cases
Conclusion: substantial evidence supports BIA/IJ that harm, even in aggregate, does not rise to persecution

outline.chapter_title: Nexus to Protected Ground: Political Opinion
outline.description: Addresses whether any harm occurred on account of petitioners’ political opinion, narrowing the nexus inquiry to political opinion because other theories were not developed.
subtopics: Scope limitation: no developed PSG argument; focus on political opinion nexus
Legal test: protected ground must be at least one central reason and not tangential or subordinate
Temporal and causal sequence: political activity continued despite early anonymous threats; escalation only after involvement in the property dispute with Don Rafa
Evidence of motive: accusations that Jimenez was a snitch for prosecutor’s office and responsible for searches; threats relayed as coming from Don Rafa
Finding: predominant motive was to protect criminal enterprise and revenue/security interests, not political opinion
Mixed-motive principle applied: political opinion at most tangential; substantial evidence standard precludes reweighing

outline.description: Evaluates whether the Colombian government was unable or unwilling to protect petitioners and whether internal relocation within Colombia was a reasonable alternative.
subtopics: Unable-or-unwilling framework: importance of reporting, governmental efforts, and protective measures
Notice to authorities: minimal reporting; conversations with two officers; absence of systemic proof of collusion or apathy
Countervailing record: prior police searches/seizures at the property undermine claim of persecutor-government alignment
Futility/danger exception: record does not compel finding reporting would be futile or dangerous
Internal relocation factors: family unharmed in Colombia; father’s ongoing justice-system employment; three-week safe stay in countryside
Threat scope: directives to leave neighborhood, not country; feasibility and reasonableness of relocation supported by record

outline.description: Summarizes the court’s holdings and highlights the practical lessons for asylum and withholding claims under Tenth Circuit law.
subtopics: Holding: petition for review denied; no past persecution, no nexus to political opinion, no showing government was unable/unwilling; safe relocation available
Withholding of removal: necessarily fails due to inability to meet lower asylum standard
Key practice points: necessity of concrete reporting or compelling futility evidence; developing PSG arguments; building evidentiary record of motive beyond criminal retaliation
Role of substantial evidence: deference to BIA/IJ where record does not compel contrary findings
Significance: case illustrates limits of threat-based claims and the impact of mixed criminal-political motives on nexus and relocation analyses
